Take a trained language model, catch it in the middle of a line of reasoning, and look inside — at the moment when the context has already turned into a column of several thousand numbers, the activation vector at some middle layer. The linear representation hypothesis asserts something almost indecently simple about this column: high-level concepts — "truth," "gender," "the language of the text," "emotional tone," "I am about to refuse to answer" — are written into it as directions. Not as cunning nonlinear patterns, not as ensembles of a thousand interacting neurons, but as straight lines in activation space. "Male→female" has a vector. "True→false" has a vector. And — here is the main promise — along these vectors one can not only read but also write: add the direction of "refusal" and the model digs in its heels; subtract it and it becomes compliant.

The classic forerunner is known even to those who have never opened a language model: the arithmetic of word2vec. `king − man + woman ≈ queen`. `Paris − France + Italy ≈ Rome`. The vector connecting "man" and "woman" turned out to be roughly the same as the one connecting "king" and "queen" — that is, "gender" lived in the embeddings as a stable offset, the same across the whole space. If this works for words, why should gender, tense, and truth not live as the same kind of directions in a transformer's deep activations too?

#### What exactly is claimed — and why it is so tempting

A careful formulation matters, because "linearity" here is treacherously ambiguous. What is meant is that for a binary concept there exists a direction v such that the projection of the activation onto v monotonically encodes the concept's value, and a shift of the activation along v causally changes the concept's value without touching the rest. From this come twin instruments. The first — linear probing: we train the simplest linear classifier on top of the activations and see whether we can read out the concept; if a linear readout works, the direction is found. The second — activation steering: we add the same direction to the activations during generation and steer behavior without any fine-tuning.

The temptation is plain. If the hypothesis is true, interpretability ceases to be hermeneutics and becomes geometry. There is no need to decipher "what the model is thinking" by peering into myriads of weights — linear algebra suffices: dot products, projections, orthogonal complements. Control, too, becomes geometry: safety is not only RLHF but also, perhaps, the subtraction of a "toxicity" vector at inference. Beautiful to the point of suspicion.

How it came about. The trail runs from distributional semantics. Mikolov and co-authors in 2013 showed regularities in word2vec — those very parallelogram analogies. It then emerged that the trick is not limited to lexical embeddings. Alain and Bengio (2016) proposed linear probes as a way of seeing what a network's intermediate layers "know." Then interpretability researchers began feeling out linear structures in the most unexpected places: Nanda and colleagues (2023) discovered that a model trained merely to predict moves in Othello contains a linearly readable board state — and in the coordinates of "my piece / opponent's piece," not "black / white." Marks and Tegmark (2023), in "The Geometry of Truth," found a direction of truth: along it true and false statements separate linearly, and a shift along it changes what the model takes to be true. Turner and co-authors (2023) turned the shift along a direction into an engineering device — Activation Addition, steering without optimization.

And then Park, Choe, and Veitch (2023–24) gave this scatter of observations a theoretical foundation: they carefully teased apart three different senses of the word "representation" (subspace, measurement by a probe, intervention), introduced the notion of the causal inner product — a metric in which causally separable concepts turn out orthogonal — and showed under what conditions a "direction" is a correct object and not an artifact of the chosen coordinate system. From folklore ("king minus man") the hypothesis became a formulable statement.

Criticism / arguments against.

First, not everything is linear. Engels, Liao, Michaud, Gurnee, and Tegmark (2024) titled their work bluntly "Not All Language Model Features Are Linear" and showed multi-dimensional features that no straight line can catch. The canonical example is cyclicity: the model lays out the days of the week and the months not along a ruler but along a circle. And for good reason — "Monday" and "Sunday" are neighbors on a cycle, not "maximum minus minimum," and the faithful geometric representation of such a concept is a circle, a two-dimensional feature, not a one-dimensional axis. Adding a "vector" to it is meaningless: along a circle there is no global direction "forward."

Second, linearity may be partial and approximate. The word2vec analogies do not always work and work worse on rare words; a truth direction found on one set of facts sometimes does not transfer to another — that is, we may be catching not "truth in general" but a correlate like "sounds plausible" or a peculiarity of the dataset. This is the flip side of superposition (Elhage et al., "Toy Models of Superposition," 2022): the model has more features than dimensions, they are packed non-orthogonally, and a naively extracted direction is almost always a mixture of several concepts. Tug at "politeness," and "formality" will move too — and so will "response length."

Third, the subtlest risk — illusory interpretability. A linear probe is trainable and greedy: give it enough dimensions and it will find a separating hyperplane for almost anything, even if the model itself does not causally use that direction. High probe accuracy proves that the information is linearly present in the activations, but not that the model relies on it. Hence a methodological discipline: probing is checked by intervention (shift along the direction — did behavior change predictably?), and steering results are checked against "placebo directions" and examined for side effects.

What to do about it / where it leads. The practical conclusion is neither "the hypothesis is true" nor "the hypothesis is false," but "linearity is a strong but leaky working model, and one must know its limits." A whole industry already stands on it: linear detector-probes (is the model lying? about to refuse? hallucinating?), activation steering as a cheap alternative to fine-tuning, representation engineering as a top-down approach to transparency. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs), the current hit of mechanistic interpretability, are the direct heirs of the hypothesis: they try to decompose superposition back into monosemantic linear features (features that each represent a single concept), in essence taking linearity as a working postulate and fighting its chief enemy — the entanglement of directions.

Where does this lead for safety? To cautious optimism with two caveats. The first caveat: do not take a found direction for a concept until you have tested its causal role and transferability; a beautiful parallelogram is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis. The second caveat: keep in mind the nonlinear and multi-dimensional "tail" — cyclic, hierarchical, branching features that a one-dimensional axis simply does not see; it is there, rather than in the convenient linear part, that whatever we end up missing is more likely to be hiding. The linear hypothesis gave alignment the dream that a machine's thoughts can be read with a ruler and edited by addition. The dream half came true — and the second half is precisely the map of where our rulers lie to us.
